source_locator.description: The prison door opens and Muthayi runs in.

notes: `அத்தான்` is retained as `Aththan` because the intimate kinship/lover address is part of the scene's register.

translation.english_text: My joy! Do not be shaken! Today is our last day! Our last meeting!... I can no longer see your eyes that sing of love! I can no longer taste the sweetness of your honey-pouring lips! Only another second or two; after that this poor Muthan can no longer carry within him the sweet memories of you!...
Aththan! No one can ever separate us—I too will come right behind you......

Hmm... madness! Some wishful fool scribbled that a world has been built for lovers and that dead lovers can settle in that world! Do not believe that and follow me! I, who am about to give up my life, ask of you only one loving command...
That you must live, without dying...
Ah!... I am one who cannot live, Aththan—I must not live any longer...

Hmm... You must not live? All kinds of people live in this wide world—are you alone not to live? The one made of baseness—the one of deceitful character—the one who breaks integrity—the one who breaks affection—the arrogant man lives too, my beauty! Are you alone not to live? The blood-mad man who raves ‘war, war’ lives too, my painted doll! Are you alone not to live? My treasure! In this world the treacherous man whose belly burns at seeing others live also lives—the heartless cruel man also lives—my diamond full moon! Are you alone not to live? The man who says one person must labour and another must flourish, while he himself came by without labour, lives happily too, Anjugame! Who said you must not live?... My life! Maykkainatha Swami, the silk-pitambara mendicant who deceives the town saying, ‘I am the Lord who performs the tandava—therefore fill this alms bowl,’ lives too—with drums and clamour and a thousand flag-bearers!
notes: The source's accumulating political and religious satire is preserved rather than softened.
`அஞ்சுகமே` is retained as the affectionate vocative `Anjugame` rather than assigned an unsupported modern gloss.
`தாண்டவம்` is retained as `tandava`; the mocked alms-bowl claim is translated only as printed.

source_locator.description: The verified derivative records that Muthan's preceding PDF 104 speech continues unlabelled on PDF 105 before Muthayi speaks.

translation.english_text: Those snakes may live, tender vine! Why should you not live?... The Vengai ruler—the megalomaniac who turned beautiful Tirunagar into Pazhuthar, plundered its gold and goods and, not satisfied with that, enslaved the very soil—lives with his henchmen and immense influence! Tribute-payers—kavadi-bearers—heralds—those who make a living washing feet—all live happily, beautiful-eyed one, on this earth!... Moon-lotus! Who said that you alone must not live?
notes: The source prints no new speaker label at the PDF 104→105 continuation. Muthan attribution remains `source-context-attributed` derivative provenance and is not manufactured as a printed label.

The supplement is represented separately because the closed source-role layer already owns this unlabelled continuation; it is not retroactively merged into the immutable explicit record `ammaiyappan-s059-d008`.

translation.english_text: Can a deer live in a tiger forest, Aththan?...

Honour is sharper than a tiger's claw, flower-vine! Songbirds that sing in the forest must live among eagles and vultures, my love! After I am gone, you too must live among this crowd of people without virtue. You must live not for yourself, but for the treasure of our love growing in your womb—the child, the fruit of nectar—the speaking golden picture. Even if I cannot see it, you are the one who will behold and rejoice in it; you are the one who must protect it!... My life, that child of joy is the one who will proclaim loudly into the ear of this world that Muthan's lineage has not been wiped out root and branch! Thinking of that future, even now I let out a sigh of happiness...
notes: The deer/tiger and songbird/predator imagery is preserved as source rhetoric.
The unborn child is described through the source's accumulating metaphors; English does not add biological or narrative detail beyond the printed speech.

translation.english_text: Do not cry, my dear! Do not cry! Let me see you once with a smiling face, so my heart may be cooled. Come, my Senthamizh! Show me a smile...
notes: `செந்தமிழே` is retained as the affectionate poetic vocative `Senthamizh` rather than flattened into an ordinary pet name.

translation.english_text: I kissed your honey-dripping lips. The world did not like it—justice, fairness—so now I am going to kiss honour! One last thing I ask, Muthayi; one last thing I ask! That love song the two of us used to sing together—where will I ever hear it again? Come, sing it once!... Sing, my dear! If you do not sing, your lover will not die in peace... Sing, my dear, sing!
notes: The source's compressed `உலகுக்கு நீதிக்கு—நியாயத்துக்கு—` sequence is rendered from its immediate rhetorical contrast without changing the frozen Tamil.

This immutable dialogue owns the source-visible request for `that love song we used to sing together` and is linked to `ammaiyappan-song-005`. The booklet prints no title, lyric body or authorship, and none is reconstructed.
